item.title: Gold dips after Fed's Waller drops the 50 bps hike bomb and US CPI comes above expectations
item.description:
Gold sold off yesterday after Fed's Waller surprised markets with some very hawkish remarks in his speech on the economic outlook.

He suggested that a rate hike in December would be warranted regardless of yesterday's inflation data, adding that the only thing the data would influence would be the size of the increase. In fact, he said that a Core CPI M/M reading of 0.3% or higher would lead him to vote for a larger 50 bps hike.

His remarks triggered a hawkish repricing, sending Treasury yields and the US dollar higher. Gold came under pressure as real yields also moved higher.

The Core CPI then came in at 0.3%, extending gold's losses as traders increased further their expectations of a 50 bps rate hike in December.

Meanwhile, nothing has changed on the US-Iran front. Qatar said yesterday that it secured at least two weeks for diplomatic efforts, adding that significant differences remain. So, the expectations for an imminent deal might need to be repriced and that should lead to a rebound in oil prices.

I would expect rate hikes to put even more downward pressure on the stock market and long-term Treasury yields going forward amid increased growth concerns, barring an end to the Iran war of course. This could ultimately be positive for gold.

Keep in mind that in the current context, if Trump decides to escalate the war, inflation expectations would rise alongside weakening growth outlook, creating a stagflationary environment. This should be bullish for gold. At the same time, if we get a de-escalation, we could see a dovish repricing on easing inflation concerns, which should also support gold in the short-term.

 

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that gold(CFD contract) is still consolidating above the broken trendline despite yesterday’s dip. The buyers piled in on the retest of the broken trendline, with a defined risk below it, targeting the 4,700 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will need to see the price breaking below the major upward trendline to open the door for new lows.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we can see more clearly yesterday’s pullback into the 4,040 support zone where we have also the confluence of the broken downward trendline and the minor upward trendline. The buyers will likely continue to step in around these levels, with a defined risk below the upward trendline, to keep targeting the 4,700 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking below the upward trendline to position for a drop into the major upward trendline next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, there’s not much we can add here as the buyers will likely continue to pile in around the support zone to keep targeting new highs, while the sellers will wait for a break below the upward trendline to extend the drop into new lows. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

item.title: European stock market open: European stocks keep the good times rolling this week
item.description:
The party continues to rock on in Europe as nobody is quite ready to turn down the music just yet this week.

European stocks are pushing higher again at the open today, carrying the more positive mood over from Asian trading. Even yesterday's hotter-than-expected US inflation numbers aren't doing much to spoil the fun, as US futures are also joining in on the festivities.

S&P 500 futures are up 0.6% while Nasdaq futures are leading the charge with a 1.5% gain. That's quite the turnaround after yesterday's inflation scare sent US stocks tumbling and Treasury yields surging. Having said that, just keep in mind though that the US bond market is closed today in observance of Veterans Day. As such, that could complicate the scenes we're seeing as equities look to be coming out of hiding amid the absence of fixed income traders.

In any case, here's how European equities are looking at the open:

  • Eurostoxx +0.9%
  • Germany DAX +0.9%
  • France CAC 40 +0.6%
  • UK FTSE +0.7%
  • Spain IBEX +0.3%
  • Italy FTSE MIB +0.7%

Regional stocks are continuing to perform well with the DAX moving closer to all-time highs once again. Germany's benchmark index is now within striking distance of its record high around 26,692, with the broader STOXX 600 also hovering near record territory.

So, what's keeping the party alive?

To start, the sharp retreat in oil prices has been a major relief for European equities. Hopes of de-escalation in the US-Iran conflict are helping to ease concerns over energy-driven inflation and that's helping to provide businesses with some added breathing room in terms of managing their costs and overlays.

Besides that, European corporate earnings have also been holding up better than feared, with banks enjoying a particularly strong start to the week. Deal-making optimism and encouraging results from the likes of UniCredit have helped lift the sector in general, so this isn't just Europe riding on Wall Street's coattails.

What looks to be telling this week is how willing investors have become to look past all of the risks from recent weeks again. But still, it is worth asking whether are we actually seeing genuine confidence returning to stocks, or are investors simply getting comfortable ignoring the risks again?

With the US bond market closed today, we won't get a proper follow-up to that until tomorrow at least. So for now, the bulls are keeping the music playing. But with European stocks starting to approach record territory once more, the question is whether there's enough fuel left to keep this party going.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Is EUR/USD heading for another breakdown or a surprise comeback?
item.description:
For well over a month now, the story in EUR/USD is that when the currency pair tries to pick itself up, sellers are seemingly waiting just around the corner to knock it back down again. And with the latest shove lower this week, you have to wonder just how much longer buyers can keep defending the floor at this rate.

The daily chart paints a rather miserable picture for buyers. Since peaking just above 1.1700 in August, it has been one-way traffic for EUR/USD as the pair entered freefall to hit a low near 1.1100 in October. More importantly, any ecent recovery attempts have repeatedly stalled around the 23.6 Fib retracement level of that very swing lower at 1.1254. That pretty much underscores the mood that sellers are showing little appetite to surrender that territory.

After being rejected once again yesterday, we are now seeing price action hover back to around 1.1150. And that once again draws in the 1.1100 level, with that looking rather vulnerable to a downside test after the dollar made a stirring comeback following the hotter-than-expected US CPI report yesterday.

The weekly chart exemplifies why the 1.1100 level is an important one to watch. The 200-week moving average (blue line) sits nearby around 1.1109 and provides an important line of defence for buyers, alongside the 50.0 Fib retracement level at 1.1129. A firm break below this support region would be a rather ominous development, potentially opening up a move towards 1.1000 next and then the 61.8 Fib retracement level at 1.0905.

That being said, can the euro still pull a rabbit out of the hat?

Well, the odds aren't exactly working in favour of the single currency I would say. Yesterday's US inflation data reinforces expectations that the Fed will have to remain on a more hawkish path, with the debate on another rate hike in December more or less settled. As for Europe, flagging growth conditions and fiscal risks arising from France are complicating the picture for the ECB in trying to make more aggressive moves going into next year.

Alongside the fact that the Fed's policy rate remains well above the ECB's, higher yields in the US will keep the dollar more attractive and thus making it more difficult for EUR/USD to stage a convincing recovery.

However, there is perhaps one little counterargument that might help the euro out. And that is positioning. According to the latest CFTC data, leveraged funds have built their largest net short euro position since early 2020 as of last week.

As such, with bearish bets already getting so crowded, any further easing in energy prices and/or improving fiscal sentiment in Europe could very well trigger a short squeeze - even without any dramatic improvement in the euro's fundamentals. So, there is that to keep in mind at least.

Looking to the week ahead, the US PPI data on Friday will be one to watch before we get to US retail sales and the Fed minutes next week.

Circling back to the charts, buyers will have to try and secure another push back above 1.1200 to try and reclaim some semblance of control to start with. However, breaking above 1.1254 is what is necessary to give any recovery some added credibility.

Until then, sellers will still hold the upper hand at the balance. And if the 1.1100 level finally gives way, things are going to get much worse for the euro before they get better.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold traders see plenty of drama after US CPI but still no clear winner for now
item.description:
It's been a back and forth kind of week for gold so far, with there being plenty of pushing and pulling in general. And we also got a little drama courtesy of the US CPI report yesterday, yet somehow we're still going around in circles - more or less. For all the excitement, we're just seemingly going back to where we started the week. Oh, what fun. Pfft.

Anyway, the hotter-than-expected inflation numbers yesterday gave sellers a reason to pounce as both the monthly headline and core inflation readings came in above estimates. That saw Treasury yields surge higher alongside the dollar, putting gold under heavy pressure as markets ramped up bets on further Fed tightening.

But despite the heavy selloff, gold managed to find support near $4,020 before bouncing back towards $4,060 today. And despite the recovery since last week, gold buyers still haven't exactly made much meaningful progress in establishing a firmer bullish footing.

Looking at the hourly chart, buyers managed to somewhat defend the 200-hour moving average (blue line) in overnight trading but are now facing a familiar resistance hurdle in the form of the 100-hour moving average (red line) next. The latter sits around $4,088 currently and offers the first key near-term test for buyers in the latest bounce today. Beyond that, the $4,140-46 region has repeatedly capped upside attempts so far this month, making it the more important near-term resistance to break.

But even then, I wouldn't be too quick to label a push above that as being a major breakthrough for gold. In the bigger picture, buyers will still have to contend with the $4,200 region, which marks another swing resistance area alongside the 100-day moving average. So until that gives way, there is little reason to suggest that the latest recovery is turning into something more convincing. But baby steps I guess.

On the flip side, sellers have a much clearer target in sight.

The weekly chart shows why the $4,000 mark remains such an important battleground. Not only is it a major psychological level, but the 100-week moving average (red line) is also sitting just below it at $3,898. That combination helped to arrest decline at the end of last month, reinforcing the area as a crucial technical support zone.

It would take a firm break below both to really shift the technical picture more decisively in favour of sellers, potentially exposing the next support around $3,500.

For now, I'm still seeing a market caught between buyers who haven't quite done enough and sellers who can't finish the job. The real question is which side can finally deliver that next meaningful technical break.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Germany October inflation slows, but winter energy risks keep ECB rate hike bets alive
item.description:
• Germany October final CPI +2.8% vs +2.8% y/y prelim
  • Prior +3.3%
  • Germany October final HICP +2.8% vs +2.8% y/y prelim
  • Prior +3.3%

The final report here pretty much confirms what we already seen with the preliminary report from earlier. The easing in price pressures in Europe's largest economy owed much to a slower increase in energy prices in October, as well as the introduction of temporary fuel tax cuts starting 1 October (scheduled to run through the end of the year). That being said, all measures of underlying inflation also fell with services and goods prices also dropping on the month.

Destatis notes that:

"The main reason for the continued high inflation rate remained the development of energy prices, even though the fuel discount, which was reintroduced at the beginning of October, likely dampened inflation somewhat."

The more crucial estimate, that being core annual inflation, is reaffirmed at 2.1% in October - marking a drop from 2.4% in September. So, that will offer some comfort to the ECB that price pressures are not exactly surging all across the region towards the final quarter of the year.

Having said that, do be reminded that we are approaching the start of the winter season. And combined with low gas storage levels, that is also likely to push up gas prices in the coming weeks. In turn, that could possibly translate into higher retail/consumer prices at the start of next year.

For now though, the inflation data will help to give ECB doves some added comfort as the numbers show that there are still no second-round effects in sight. But while the data may suggest that a December rate hike is not a done deal just yet, the stronger inflation pressures elsewhere are likely to tip the scales in the favour of another move by year-end. And market odds are reaffirming that, with a roughly 79% probability being priced in for a 25 bps rate hike in December currently.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Heads up: US bond market closed for Veterans Day as stocks face a hot CPI hangover
item.description:
Talk about picking an awkward time to take a day off, eh?

Wall Street was left licking its wounds yesterday after the hotter-than-expected US inflation data sent Treasury yields surging and stocks tumbling. And just as traders are trying to make sense of the fallout, the bond market is going to be off on a holiday.

A reminder and a quick heads up that today is Veterans Day in the US, meaning the bond market will be closed while stock markets will remain open as per usual.

As such, that makes for a rather peculiar setup after yesterday's market reaction to the inflation numbers.

Headline inflation came in at 0.4% m/m in October against the 0.3% expected, while core inflation rose by 0.3% m/m versus estimates of 0.2%. And that was enough to reignite concerns over the Fed potentially having to tighten policy more aggressively in December, especially after Fed governor Waller warned about perhaps needing to move by 50 bps on stronger price pressures than anticipated.

The bond market reaction was jarring. 2-year Treasury yields jumped by roughly 18 bps to 4.74%, while 10-year yields climbed by around 12 bps to to settle at 5%. In turn, equities weren't too pleased with the S&P 500 falling 0.4% and the Nasdaq shedding 0.7%. But for a late recovery, the selloff in stocks would've been much worse.

So, what does that mean for trading today?

With the bond market and fixed income traders out of action, we won't have the usual response from Treasury yields to help gauge whether yesterday's inflation shock is being digested or repriced further.

Taking that into consideration, I suspect that could leave broader markets trading with less conviction, particularly as some institutional participants also step away for the holiday. Having said that, let's not mistake quieter conditions for being an absence of risk. Thinner liquidity can also exaggerate moves when larger orders hit the market, especially if equities continue to struggle. So, just keep that in mind.

For the European morning session to follow, I'd be keeping an eye on US futures, the dollar and whether tech stocks can find their footing before we get to the Wall Street open later.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq Today says: "Fold that short."
item.description:
Opinion: You don't want to be shorting this market (Nasdaq) when the price has reclaimed this channel (daily timeframe).

Nasdaq futures may be reversing the selloff. Here's where the bullish case could fail

After last week's technology-stock rout, Nasdaq futures are showing early signs of a bullish recovery. Improving price action and buying pressure suggest that sellers may be losing control, but the critical question is whether buyers can defend the recovery or whether another sharp decline is coming.

Nasdaq-100 futures (NQ) are beginning to challenge the bearish narrative that dominated last week's technology-stock selloff. The latest price and order-flow evidence favors an early bullish recovery, but not a confirmed long-term reversal. For traders, the area around 27,780-27,813 could be particularly important in determining whether the recovery survives.

And there is an important lesson here: You can be right about the direction of the Nasdaq and still lose money by buying at the wrong time.

Is the Nasdaq selloff turning into something more bullish?

The sharp technology-stock decline on Thursday, November 5, left many investors questioning whether the market was entering a deeper correction.

Concerns surrounding artificial intelligence spending, stretched valuations and the financial demands of AI infrastructure have made investors especially sensitive to weakness in companies such as Nvidia.

But markets rarely move in straight lines, and the evidence is starting to change.

Nasdaq futures recovered significantly after reaching approximately 26,366.50 on November 6. Another decline toward 27,516 on November 10 failed to produce a sustained breakdown.

The subsequent recovery was accompanied by improving hourly price action and increasingly constructive buying pressure.

By approximately 00:29 Eastern Time on November 11, NQ was trading around 28,227, having reached an observed high of 28,233.25.

Those are historical overnight observations, not continuously updated market quotations.

What interests me is not simply that Nasdaq futures have rebounded. It is how the market has behaved when sellers attempted to push prices lower, and how effectively buyers subsequently advanced the price.

The AI rebound is spreading beyond Wall Street

There are other developments worth connecting to the futures picture.

In Asia, technology shares have been recovering. South Korea's KOSDAQ has jumped nearly 5%, adding to evidence that appetite for some AI-related investments is returning.

The broader regional developments are covered in investingLive's Asia-Pacific market news report on the KOSDAQ rebound and oil markets.

Meanwhile, CoreWeave stock surged approximately 13% following its earnings announcement.

The company's strong revenue growth and higher guidance provide evidence that demand for AI computing infrastructure remains substantial.

However, as the CoreWeave analysis explains, extraordinary growth does not eliminate concerns about financing costs or guarantee a sustainable stock-price recovery.

This distinction is important.

Investors can become more optimistic about AI infrastructure demand while remaining concerned about profitability, valuations and financing.

Similarly, improving sentiment toward AI stocks can help Nasdaq futures recover without guaranteeing that the broader market has established a durable bullish trend.

There is also a macroeconomic complication. The October US consumer price index, released November 10, increased 0.4% month over month, with core inflation rising 0.3%.

Inflation and interest-rate expectations remain meaningful risks for growth-stock valuations.

Something interesting is happening beneath the Nasdaq recovery

One of the most useful ways to assess a market recovery is to compare price movement with the buying and selling activity taking place beneath it.

An important observation occurred during the 10:00 a.m. Eastern hour on November 10.

Nasdaq futures advanced approximately 362 points, despite recording negative net trading Delta.

What does that mean?

Delta measures the difference between aggressive buying volume and aggressive selling volume.

A negative Delta means that more volume was executed aggressively on the selling side than on the buying side.

Yet prices advanced.

That apparent contradiction teaches us something important: Aggressive selling does not automatically produce falling prices.

The market's response to buying and selling pressure can sometimes be more informative than the pressure itself.

In the subsequent recovery, several hourly advances were accompanied by increasingly consistent positive Delta.

That is a more straightforward bullish combination. Buyers were becoming more aggressive, and prices were responding by moving higher.

Additional positive buying-pressure observations during the November 10 evening session strengthened the case that the recovery was attracting participation.

However, the latest completed Delta observations preceded the final upward extension in the price data. That extension should not be described as independently confirmed by fresh Delta readings.

None of this proves institutional accumulation or guarantees another rally.

It does suggest that the bearish conditions visible during last week's selloff are no longer behaving quite the same way.

Nasdaq futures: The 27,780-27,813 area deserves attention

This is probably the most practical part of the analysis for swing traders.

Two important market references from November 10 are relatively close together:

27,780: Previous-session Point of Control

The Point of Control, or POC, identifies the price associated with the highest trading volume within a defined volume profile.

It helps illustrate where substantial trading activity was concentrated.

27,813: Previous-session VWAP

VWAP stands for Volume-Weighted Average Price. It measures the average trading price, weighted by volume.

Traders use it to assess whether the market is trading above or below an important volume-weighted reference.

Together, these measurements establish an area around 27,780-27,813 that could help distinguish a healthy recovery from a potentially failing one.

If Nasdaq futures remain comfortably above this region, the early bullish interpretation retains meaningful support.

But sustained trading below the area would make me reconsider whether buyers are really establishing control.

The distinction between a temporary penetration and sustained trading below support matters.

A sharp downward move that quickly reverses is not necessarily equivalent to a breakdown that holds and attracts further selling.

What about 27,600?

There is a wider reference around 27,600, just below a previous-session value-area boundary near 27,619.

For traders evaluating a broader swing, that provides additional room for volatility.

But there is a trade-off.

Using wider structural tolerance means accepting substantially more movement against a bullish view before deciding that the recovery may be failing.

For my early-reversal interpretation, I prefer paying attention to the 27,780-27,813 region rather than automatically allowing the market all the way down to 27,600 before reconsidering.

These are analytical reference levels, not universal stop-loss instructions.

The most important trading lesson: Being early versus being right

Imagine two traders examining the same Nasdaq recovery.

The first wants substantial confirmation before considering a bullish position.

The second is willing to explore the bullish possibility earlier, accepting the risk that the apparent reversal may fail.

Neither approach is automatically superior.

The first trader may avoid several false starts, but also risk entering only after much of the rally has happened.

The second may obtain more favorable positioning, but may experience more failed reversal attempts.

There is no free lunch.

Now consider another situation.

A trader reads a bullish Nasdaq analysis when futures are near 28,300.

The trader buys immediately, without considering how far the market has already advanced.

Nasdaq subsequently pulls back toward 28,100 or 28,000.

The bullish market interpretation might still be reasonable. But the trader could already be facing an uncomfortable loss, particularly when using leveraged futures.

This is why we should separate two different decisions:

  1. Market direction: Is the evidence becoming more bullish or bearish?

  2. Trade execution: Is the current price attractive enough, relative to the risk and potential reward, to justify a position?

A bullish outlook is not an instruction to chase a rally.

Sometimes the better decision is to wait for a pullback, a successful retest of support, or further confirmation.

And sometimes the market simply moves higher without providing the entry a trader wanted.

Missing a move does not automatically make waiting the wrong decision.

Three scenarios for Nasdaq futures

1. The bullish recovery gains strength

If NQ establishes sustained trading above approximately 28,233-28,250, that would provide another encouraging indication.

Constructive hourly closes and continued positive buying pressure would strengthen the interpretation.

The next historical upside references include approximately 28,465 and the November 4 high around 28,969.

These are areas to monitor, not guaranteed price targets.

2. Sellers regain control

A decline beneath approximately 28,060-28,100 would be an initial warning that short-term momentum is deteriorating.

More importantly, sustained trading beneath 27,780-27,813 would weaken the preferred early bullish framework.

Further weakness below 27,600 would represent a more substantial deterioration.

The November 10 low around 27,516 would then become another relevant downside reference.

In that situation, the bullish interpretation needs to change with the evidence, rather than being defended simply because it once looked promising.

3. Nasdaq consolidates instead

A third outcome is that Nasdaq moves sideways without establishing meaningful new highs or breaking important support.

Buying and selling pressure may alternate while prices remain within a range.

That is not necessarily bullish or bearish.

It may simply mean the market has not yet decided which direction it wants to pursue.

For traders, doing nothing can be a perfectly reasonable response when there is no attractive opportunity with clearly defined risk.

What does this mean for Nvidia and other technology stocks?

Nasdaq futures can offer useful clues about investors' broader appetite for growth and technology exposure.

A sustained improvement in Nasdaq price action could encourage investors to investigate whether selling pressure is also easing in individual technology stocks.

But we should not confuse the two.

A bullish Nasdaq recovery does not automatically mean Nvidia, CoreWeave, Microsoft or every other technology company will rise.

Their earnings, valuations, financial positions and individual technical structures still matter.

CoreWeave's post-earnings volatility illustrates the point particularly well. An individual company can experience dramatic price movements even while the broader index follows a different path.

Futures can help establish market context, but they should complement rather than replace stock-specific analysis.

My conclusion: The bears may be losing their advantage, but don't confuse that with a buy signal

The Nasdaq's recent recovery has developed beyond a single positive candle.

We have improving hourly price action, signs that aggressive selling is producing less sustained downside progress, and increasingly constructive buying pressure.

Taken together, these observations make me less comfortable with the assumption that aggressively shorting Nasdaq remains the better side of the market.

That does not mean another selloff is impossible.

The broader technical damage has not been fully repaired, and investors continue to face genuine uncertainties involving AI spending, inflation and technology valuations.

For now, the 27,780-27,813 area provides an important reference for assessing the health of the early recovery. Around 27,600 offers a wider structural boundary.

The bigger lesson, however, applies to virtually any market.

Good trading analysis is not about being certain of what happens next. It is about recognizing when the evidence changes, knowing what would invalidate your interpretation, and understanding that a promising market direction does not automatically provide an attractive trade entry.

Market analysis based on Nasdaq futures observations through November 11, 2026, 00:29 ET. The outlook is conditional and should be reassessed as new trading data become available.

Educational only. Trade at your own risk.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Euro bears haven't been this aggressive since the Covid pandemic, but is the trade getting too crowded?
item.description:
The euro certainly isn't winning any popularity contests these days. A fragile growth outlook alongside surging energy prices and growing fiscal concerns in France has left traders with little reason to cheer for the single currency.

And judging by the latest CFTC positioning data, leveraged funds aren't just turning their backs on the euro as well. They're practically racing each other to bet against it. But when a consensus trade becomes too heavy and one-sided, there's always the risk that it can get a little too crowded for comfort.

That is precisely what MUFG is warning about in highlighting that speculative short positions in the euro have now reached their highest level since the Covid pandemic in early 2020. The latest CFTC positioning data shows that leveraged funds are holding a net short position of 78,559 euro futures contracts as of 3 November. That is up sharply from just 28,156 contracts in mid-September.

MUFG notes that:

"The recent unfavourable combination of higher energy prices and government borrowing costs particularly in France has reinforced euro selling pressure. The release of the latest IMM positioning report at the end of last week revealed leveraged funds are heavily short the euro."

As mentioned, the bearish sentiment on the single currency isn't all too surprising. Europe's energy vulnerability has returned to be a hot topic amid the US-Iran conflict, with higher oil prices threatening to make the ECB's inflation headache even worse.

Then you throw in surging borrowing costs in France and the picture gets even messier. Investors are now having to contend with fiscal uncertainty just as the region faces another potential hit to economic growth.

That being said, MUFG does see some scope for relief if oil prices continue to ease amid hopes of de-escalation in the US-Iran conflict. The firm argues that the euro would be "vulnerable to a short squeeze in the near-term if the investor concerns over the scale of the energy shock continue to fade".

Now, that doesn't automatically make the euro a good buy. It is best to remember that the underlying economic challenges haven't suddenly disappeared. However, the problem for euro bears is that they don't necessarily need to.

With positioning already this stretched, even a modest improvement in sentiment could force leveraged funds to unwind their short positions. And that could potentially give EUR/USD a platform for a sharper bounce more than the fundamentals alone might justify.

Despite the potential for some relief, MUFG is still maintaining its year-end target for EUR/USD at 1.12 though. So, that still does speak to their overall conviction on the euro even though there is scope for a positioning bounce.

I would say that the next set of clues will come from whether oil prices stay lower, French-German bond yield spreads narrow further and the next CFTC report shows any meaningful short covering.

With bearish positioning already at its most extreme since the Covid pandemic, I suspect the bigger risk for traders now isn't necessarily being wrong about the euro's outlook. It is more so being caught on the wrong side of the trade when everyone decides to head for the exit at once - even if temporarily.

item.title: Three reasons Goldman has added another Fed rate hike to its forecast, higher and higher!
item.description:
A tier-one bank moving to three hikes in the cycle supports the US dollar and front-end Treasury yields, and adds to pressure on rate-sensitive equities and gold. Pushing the first cut back to December 2027 extends the period of restrictive policy, which could weigh on long-duration assets. The reversal of Goldman’s late-October call also shows how much oil is driving the outlook: the Middle East escalation it flagged as a risk has fed directly into the inflation data. Further gains in crude, including from attacks on Hormuz shipping and Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, would raise the odds of the hike coming in January rather than March.

---

Three hot inflation prints have turned Goldman’s “maybe” on a March hike back into a “likely”.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs still expects a 25bp Fed hike in December and has added another 25bp hike in March 2027
  • The March move could come in January, but March is slightly more likely given expected milder November and December inflation data
  • Goldman pushed its forecast for the first rate cut back a quarter, to December 2027
  • It expects most FOMC members to signal a third hike in the December dot plot
  • The bank still sees inflation meaningfully lower by end-2027 as tariff, energy and AI pressures fade

Goldman Sachs now expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again in March 2027, following a quarter-point hike in December, after a third consecutive month of hotter-than-expected inflation data, the bank’s chief US economist David Mericle said in a note on Tuesday.

Goldman continues to forecast a 25 basis point increase at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting, which would be the second hike of the current tightening cycle. The new March call adds a third. Mericle said the move could be brought forward to January, but March is slightly more likely. Inflation readings for November and December are expected to be relatively mild, while larger price increases early in the year are likely to lift January’s figures. The bank also pushed back its forecast for the first rate cut by a quarter, to December 2027.

The change follows October’s consumer price report, which showed a larger-than-expected rise. Goldman expects the run of firm inflation data to lead most Fed policymakers to signal a third hike in the December dot plot, and said a strong January inflation report would make delivering that hike the path of least resistance. The bank remains confident, however, that inflation will be meaningfully lower by the end of 2027 as the effects of tariffs, the energy shock and AI-related price pressures fade.

The forecast reverses a call Goldman made only weeks ago. In late October, the bank had removed a March hike from its base case. It warned at the time that an escalation in the Middle East that drove oil prices higher, combined with persistent inflation, could change the Fed’s path. Its asset management arm has also cautioned that hotter inflation could force a more aggressive tightening cycle extending into 2027.

Goldman’s revised outlook is broadly in line with Fed commentary this week. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said further gradual hikes seem appropriate, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called the CPI report borderline disturbing, and Governor Christopher Waller had said a hot reading could lead him to back a larger move. Markets are pricing a quarter-point December hike as close to certain, with a small chance of a half-point move.

With the federal funds target range currently at 3.75% to 4%, December’s decision and its updated projections will show whether policymakers are ready to signal the further tightening Goldman expects.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morgan Stanley’s Wilson: correction in final phase, three reasons oil can fall into 2027
item.description:
A major-bank strategist calling the correction’s final phase gives dip buyers support, especially alongside the post-midterm seasonal record. Oil is the key link. If Brent and WTI keep falling on demand destruction and new non-Hormuz supply, that would ease inflation pressure and could temper Fed hike expectations, a significant shift from oil as the main inflation risk this year. The flip side is that any renewed escalation in the Middle East would quickly undercut his thesis. His target range near current levels suggests limited further downside in his view, but his warning against timing the bottom points to more volatility first.

---

Wilson says the worst of the correction is nearly done, and the next tailwind for stocks could be the oil price that has troubled them all year.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley’s Michael Wilson told CNBC that the stock market correction is entering its final phase
  • He gave a 7,100 to 7,300 target range for the S&P 500, which he said is already close
  • He cited a sharp deterioration in market breadth as evidence of late-stage correction, but warned against timing the bottom
  • He said the six to 12 months after midterm elections have historically been very strong
  • Brent has fallen 16% and WTI 12% in recent trading, and he expects further falls on demand destruction and new supply away from Hormuz

The stock market correction is entering its final phase, and a significant decline in oil prices could set up a positive backdrop for equities heading into 2027, Morgan Stanley chief investment officer and chief US equity strategist Michael Wilson told CNBC on Tuesday.

Wilson said the S&P 500 has finally begun to catch down to what he called a “pretty devastating correction under the surface”. He was referring to weakness that had already spread across much of the market before it showed up in the headline index. He gave a target range of 7,100 to 7,300 for the index and said it is already close to that zone.

As evidence that the correction is in its late stages, Wilson pointed to a sharp deterioration in market breadth across the whole market. He cautioned, however, that investors should not try to time the exact bottom.

Wilson also highlighted the market’s record after midterm elections, saying the six to 12 months following a midterm have historically been very strong. He urged investors not to second-guess that pattern despite recent volatility.

Oil is central to his view. Brent crude has fallen 16% and WTI 12% in recent trading, and Wilson attributed part of the decline to easing concerns about military conflict, describing it as a potentially very positive driver into 2027.

He expects further falls. Part of the move reflects demand destruction after the price spike, Wilson said, but he also expects a supply response, as energy-insecure countries look for alternatives to relying on oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz. That means more drilling and more energy infrastructure, he said, which he sees as a further positive for markets. Wilson said he personally thinks oil will come down quite a bit, for reasons beyond the easing of conflict risk.

For investors, his message was patience. In Wilson’s view, the correction’s final stages, combined with lower energy costs and a supportive post-midterm pattern, set up favourable conditions for equities into 2027.

His comments echo the midterm argument made this week by Morgans’ Jack Stickley, and point to a shift in focus from oil as an inflation risk to oil as a potential tailwind for stocks. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: CoreWeave stock jumps nearly 13% after earnings. Buy the rally or sell into resistance?
item.description:
CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) surged approximately 12.6% in overnight trading following its November 10 earnings, but the advance was anything but straightforward. The stock initially rallied, nearly surrendered its gains, and then recovered dramatically. For traders deciding whether to buy, sell or wait, what happened between those moves may be more important than the final percentage gain.

Why CoreWeave's earnings matter for the entire AI trade

The results arrive at an unusually sensitive moment for AI investors.

There's a growing debate about whether enormous spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure will produce adequate financial returns. Demand for computing power may be extraordinary, but investors increasingly want to know who will finance the expansion, at what cost, and when the investment will translate into sustainable profits.

I'm keeping a close eye on the broader AI and data-centre trade this week, as structural constraints and massive capital flows are colliding to create serious volatility. On the supply side, we're about to see a major gauge of retail appetite with Anthropic allocating up to 20% of its massive $64 billion IPO directly to retail investors.

Meanwhile, the physical limitations of scaling AI capacity are starting to hit balance sheets, highlighted by SoftBank swinging to a massive $7 billion Q2 loss following a brutal $3.7 billion hit on US data centre power equipment.

Despite these infrastructure bottlenecks, the underlying compute demand remains red-hot, evidenced by CoreWeave beating on every major Q3 metric and lifting its 2026 revenue guidance to $13.3 billion on the back of strengthening margins.

However, the overarching semiconductor sentiment is feeling the weight of the tech sell-off, and my primary focus on the charts right now is how Nvidia reacts as it sheds another 6% to test a critical long-term support zone around those March 2026 and September 2025 lows (that may be the area of the dip for Nvida, folks, it's up 2.3% in Overnight trading after CoreWeave's pop). I'll be tracking if that holds in pre-market of Wed, 11 Nov.

Back to CoreWeave earning...

CoreWeave Q3 2026 results and guidance

Q3 revenue$3.66 billion (+168% YoY)

Q3 operating income$207 million

Q3 net interest expense$846 million

Q3 net loss$709 million

2026 revenue guidance$13.0-$13.3 billion

2026 capex guidance$37-$39 billion

Expected Q4 interest expense$1.05-$1.15 billion

Source: CoreWeave Q3 2026 earnings release, November 10, 2026.

Notice that quarterly net interest expense exceeded operating income by more than four times. This is one reason investors can celebrate the operating performance while remaining concerned about the company's financial structure.

According to Reuters, CoreWeave's management has pointed to approximately $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected over the coming three months as a source of funding. That could help ease near-term financing pressure, although the money remains expected rather than already received.

Another complication: Nvidia and investor confidence

The backdrop also includes the controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

On November 8, Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation following reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The company emphasized that it had no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets had been compromised and expressed confidence in Huang's leadership.

The significance for markets is not that the controversy changes CoreWeave's contracts or Nvidia's technology overnight. It is that uncertainty concerning one of the AI industry's most important leaders arrives while investors are already reassessing the sector's valuations, financing requirements and growth assumptions.

CoreWeave therefore offers an interesting additional test of AI market sentiment.

If investors embrace its strong financial results despite the financing concerns and broader uncertainty, that could provide some reassurance to other AI infrastructure stocks. A failed earnings rally, on the other hand, would suggest that investors remain reluctant to pay higher prices for growth without greater financial certainty.

Neither outcome would, by itself, settle the wider AI investment debate.

The most interesting part of CoreWeave's earnings rally is what almost went wrong

CoreWeave closed the November 10 regular session at $48.73.

Following the earnings announcement, shares initially surged toward $54. That seemed encouraging for buyers.

Then the stock surrendered most of those gains, with the initial earnings-hour candle closing around $49.23.

But the real test came next.

Sellers pushed CoreWeave below its pre-earnings close, reaching approximately $46.50.

Imagine being a trader watching this unfold. First the stock surges, encouraging buyers to chase the move. Then the rally collapses, and the stock trades below where it stood before the earnings announcement.

That looks like a potential opportunity for sellers.

Except the breakdown didn't hold.

CRWV recovered above $48.73, subsequently closed an hourly candle at $50.15, and continued moving higher. Later completed hourly closes reached $51.66, $52.58 and eventually $54.87.

THE EARNINGS REACTION

Pre-earnings close

$48.73

Breakdown low

$46.50

Hourly recovery close

$54.87

Historical extended-hours observations, not regular-session closing prices. The $54.87 close was approximately 12.6% above the November 10 regular-session close.

This is where we get an important technical-analysis lesson.

It wasn't merely that buyers pushed the price higher.

Sellers also had an opportunity to take control, but they could not sustain the move below the pre-earnings closing price. The subsequent recovery offered evidence that short-term buying pressure was strengthening.

In technical analysis, this is often described as a failed breakdown.

A failed breakdown can be useful because it tells us something about how price behaves when sellers challenge an important area. It does not prove which traders were buying, whether anyone was forced to cover short positions, or that a lasting reversal is assured.

The lesson: Watch how the market reacts to its own reaction, not just the first move following an earnings announcement.

CRWV's chart was improving even before earnings

The hourly chart also shows a potentially important change in price structure.

Previously, CoreWeave had been making lower highs. That is a simple characteristic of a declining trend: rallies repeatedly run out of momentum before reaching the preceding peaks.

The purple descending trendline on the supplied chart helps visualize that weakness.

After CRWV touched approximately $40.58 on November 5, however, its recovery began producing higher lows.

Eventually, price moved above the descending trendline.

That is the first encouraging technical development, but it is not sufficient on its own to declare a new bull market.

The next clue is the formation of an ascending channel, represented by the two rising blue lines.

The lower boundary describes where buyers have tended to support the recovering price. The upper boundary identifies an area where the advance may encounter resistance.

For a trader, the value of recognizing this pattern is straightforward: it provides context.

Even if your strategy does not specifically trade channels, knowing that price is advancing within a rising structure can help you assess whether a short position is fighting the prevailing recovery, or whether a proposed long entry is already close to resistance.

And that brings us to the next critical test.

CoreWeave stock: The $55.60-$56.55 area could decide the next move

The supplied research identifies three important price regions.

$55.60-$56.55: Immediate resistance

The overnight rally reached approximately $55.65, directly inside this area. The region also overlaps prior price resistance, including the November 2 high near $55.74.

A brief move above resistance does not establish a successful breakout. Buyers need to demonstrate that they can sustain higher prices rather than immediately surrendering the advance.

A convincing move beyond this area would strengthen the case for continued recovery and potentially bring $58-$60 into focus as another area to investigate.

$53.60-$54.14: First important support region

If CoreWeave pulls back after the overnight surge, this is one area to watch.

The most constructive development would be a pullback that stabilizes, holds support and subsequently attracts renewed buying.

That would offer evidence that the earnings recovery is developing beyond its initial burst of enthusiasm.

$50.70-$52.10: Deeper recovery support

A larger decline toward this region would not necessarily mean the recovery has failed. Earnings reactions can involve substantial volatility, especially in a stock such as CoreWeave.

However, repeated failures to rebound and sustained trading beneath this area would weaken the short-term bullish interpretation.

The $48.73 pre-earnings close remains another particularly meaningful reference. A sustained move back below it would challenge the proposition that buyers have maintained control since the earnings announcement.

How could traders approach CoreWeave after the earnings pop?

There is more than one reasonable response to a stock that has just advanced nearly 13%.

The important distinction is between having a directional opinion and having a trade with an acceptable entry, risk and potential reward.

Scenario 1: Buying a confirmed breakout

Traders who favor momentum may be interested if CRWV moves convincingly above $55.60-$56.55.

But the key word is convincingly.

A price spike above the region followed by a rapid reversal is very different from a breakout that sustains higher trading levels.

Some traders may prefer to wait for a retest, where price returns toward the former resistance area and demonstrates that buyers are willing to defend it as support.

The benefit is additional evidence. The disadvantage is that the stock might continue without offering a favorable entry.

Neither outcome should be assumed in advance.

Scenario 2: Buying a pullback rather than chasing

A trader attracted by the improving trend might prefer to see whether CRWV holds $53.60-$54.14 or, following a deeper correction, $50.70-$52.10.

That can potentially offer a more favorable relationship between entry price and risk than buying immediately into overhead resistance.

However, support is not guaranteed.

An attractive pullback requires evidence that selling pressure is diminishing and that buyers can regain control. A price reaching a support region is not automatically an entry signal.

Scenario 3: Selling into strength or considering a bearish trade

The opposite possibility is that CRWV reaches $55.60-$56.55 and fails to establish a sustainable breakout.

For a trader already holding a profitable position, this could be an area to assess partial profit-taking, depending on the original investment plan.

For bearish traders, repeated rejection near resistance followed by a loss of $53.60-$54.14 would provide stronger evidence than simply shorting because the stock appears to have risen too much.

The $50.70-$52.10 region would then become relevant as a potential further downside test.

The distinction matters: selling shares you already own is not the same decision as opening a new short position. Shorting a volatile stock immediately after earnings adds significant reversal and execution risk.

None of these scenarios provides a complete trade order. Actual entries, stops, position sizes and exits must be established against the chosen setup and its invalidation.

A warning from CoreWeave's previous earnings: A big rally can still fail

There is an especially useful historical comparison.

Following CoreWeave's August 11, 2026, earnings announcement, the stock closed the next regular trading session at $107.73, up approximately 19.3% from its $90.32 pre-earnings close.

That was a much larger initial positive reaction than the current overnight advance.

Yet by August 20, CRWV had fallen to $89.76, below its pre-earnings closing price.

Think about what that means.

A trader who bought the initial earnings rally and interpreted it as proof of a sustainable reversal would have faced a substantial subsequent decline.

The August example does not predict that November's rally will fail. It is one historical observation, not a statistical forecast.

But it illustrates why it can be dangerous to confuse an initial positive earnings reaction with a lasting change in the market's assessment of a company.

A good earnings report, a strong initial rally and a durable bullish trend are three different things.

What CoreWeave could tell us about Nvidia and the broader market

There is one more dimension worth watching.

During the observed post-earnings recovery, CRWV showed substantial relative strength against Nasdaq-100 futures in the supplied research.

That supports the view that the move was more than a routine advance alongside the broader technology market, although the comparison is not adjusted for CoreWeave's much greater volatility.

For a wider perspective, traders should monitor whether Nvidia and other AI infrastructure names demonstrate improving price action during the regular session.

It would also be useful to compare the response in CoreWeave's debt with its equity.

If the stock rallies but credit investors continue demanding unusually high yields, that divergence would suggest that equity optimism has not fully resolved financing concerns.

Conversely, evidence of improving borrowing conditions alongside better earnings and positive price action would make the recovery more compelling for longer-term investors.

The reaction to CoreWeave's results could influence sentiment toward the wider AI infrastructure industry. But it should not be treated as a definitive forecast for Nvidia or the Nasdaq.

So, is CoreWeave stock a buy or sell after earnings?

The evidence favors a cautiously constructive assessment of the short-term technical recovery, not an unconditional buy recommendation.

The stock has broken its previous descending trendline, developed a rising channel and recovered from a failed post-earnings breakdown.

Those are meaningful bullish observations.

However, CRWV is approaching resistance after a substantial overnight move. The company also faces financing demands that cannot be dismissed simply because revenue growth is exceptional.

For short-term traders, the most valuable question is whether buyers can defend the recovery and establish sustained trading above $55.60-$56.55.

For investors considering a longer holding period, the critical question extends beyond the next few candles. Can CoreWeave convert its enormous backlog into revenue and cash flow quickly enough, and at sufficient profitability, to justify the capital it requires?

Those are related questions, but they operate on different timescales.

My central takeaway is that the most interesting part of the CoreWeave earnings rally wasn't the initial jump. It was the failed selloff that followed, and the buyers' ability to recover.

Now those buyers face another challenge: proving that the recovery can survive the next regular trading session.

That is where the more meaningful evidence begins.

Educational only. Trade at your own risk.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Three forecasts that show why BofA thinks the memory chip boom can avoid a 2028 bust
item.description:
The call supports the view that memory, and HBM in particular, remains one of the strongest earnings stories in the AI supply chain, which helps memory makers and chip equipment suppliers after the recent tech sell-off. The gap between TrendForce’s and BofA’s price assumptions is the key risk for investors: if BofA’s earlier-correction scenario plays out, 2027 earnings forecasts across the sector may need to come down. Long-term supply agreements reducing volatility beyond 2028 would challenge the industry’s traditional boom-bust pattern, and could justify higher valuation multiples. The outlook also ties in with today’s UBS and SoftBank notes, which highlighted data centre power and policy as constraints on the AI build-out.

--

TrendForce and BofA agree the memory boom has legs, but differ widely on prices, and that gap is where the risk lies.

Summary:

  • BofA says the memory upcycle could last through 2027 and avoid a downturn in 2028, citing TrendForce’s Avril Wu
  • Wu expects Q4 DRAM and HBM prices to rise 10% to 20% quarter on quarter, and NAND to rise 8% to 13%
  • She sees HBM prices more than doubling in 2027, with long-term supply deals reducing volatility beyond 2028
  • BofA is more cautious: Q4 DRAM up 8%, NAND up 3%, HBM gains in 2027 below 50%, and corrections possibly starting earlier in 2027
  • BofA forecasts memory industry revenue of $970 billion in 2026, $1.47 trillion in 2027 and $1.58 trillion in 2028

The memory chip industry’s current upcycle could last through 2027 and avoid a downturn in 2028, Bank of America said, citing comments from TrendForce’s Avril Wu during a BofA-hosted webcast on November 10.

Wu said memory prices were likely to keep climbing. She expects DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) prices to rise 10% to 20% in the fourth quarter of 2026 from the previous quarter, with NAND flash prices up 8% to 13%. Looking further out, she sees HBM prices more than doubling in 2027. She also said long-term supply agreements between chipmakers and customers could help reduce price swings beyond 2028.

BofA broadly shares the bullish outlook but is more cautious on pricing. The bank expects fourth-quarter DRAM prices to rise 8% on the quarter and NAND prices 3%, both well below TrendForce’s ranges. It also sees HBM price increases in 2027 staying below 50%, far short of the doubling Wu expects, and warned that price corrections could begin earlier in 2027.

Even on those more conservative assumptions, BofA’s numbers point to a historic run. The bank forecasts global memory industry revenue of $970 billion in 2026, rising to $1.47 trillion in 2027 and $1.58 trillion in 2028. That trajectory suggests the industry could sustain record revenue and earnings through 2028, rather than slipping into the kind of downturn that has followed previous memory booms.

The debate matters because memory has become one of the tightest links in the AI supply chain. HBM is stacked alongside AI processors to feed them data at high speed, which makes it central to the build-out of AI data centres, and its pricing power has been a major driver of earnings across the sector. The gap between TrendForce’s and BofA’s assumptions shows how much uncertainty remains about how long that pricing power lasts.

TrendForce is a Taipei-based market intelligence firm that tracks the global technology supply chain, with a particular focus on semiconductors, memory and displays. Its DRAMeXchange division is one of the most widely cited sources for DRAM and NAND contract and spot pricing. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morgans’ Stickley: S&P 500 up after every midterm since 1950 as Nvidia looks cheap
item.description:
A strong post-midterm seasonal record gives dip buyers a historical anchor, but the AI sell-off shows that policy risk to the data centre build-out is now a live variable for tech valuations. Nvidia’s results next week are the near-term test: guidance of more than $100 billion in revenue would back the view that fundamentals have decoupled from the share price. Stickley’s link between the election result and lower oil prices matters for the inflation outlook. If oil keeps easing, it could temper Fed hike expectations, which would support equities. For now that is his interpretation, not an established trend.

---

History says buy the post-midterm dip, and Morgans’ Stickley is doing so carefully, with Nvidia’s results next week the first real test.

Summary:

  • Morgans’ Jack Stickley told ausbiz that the S&P 500 has risen in the six and 12 months after every midterm election since 1950, by about 14% and 15%
  • He sees the Democratic sweep of Congress reining in parts of Trump’s agenda rather than derailing markets
  • He said the chip sell-off followed a very strong run and elevated valuations, but fundamentals remain strong
  • Nvidia has a large backlog, guidance of more than $100 billion in quarterly revenue and a forward P/E around 11 times, he said
  • He is adding to tech gradually ahead of Nvidia’s results next week, and favours building positions on pullbacks

The historical pattern of US stocks rallying after midterm elections remains intact despite Wall Street’s sharp technology sell-off, Jack Stickley of Australian stockbroker Morgans said in an interview with ausbiz.

Since 1950, the S&P 500 has risen in both the six-month and 12-month periods following every US midterm election, Stickley said, with gains of about 14% and 15% respectively. He noted that a clean sweep of Congress by the party opposing the president has happened before, citing the Clinton era. In his view, the result mainly reins in parts of President Donald Trump’s policy agenda rather than changing the market’s direction. If the historical trend holds, he said, investors could be in for a good six to 12 months.

Stickley believes the election outcome has also reshaped the macro backdrop. He said voters had pushed back against the US data centre build-out and the war, and that Democratic control of both the Senate and the House creates an incentive to end the conflict, which he said had sent oil prices lower.

On technology, Stickley acknowledged the scale of the recent sell-off. He described a sudden one-day slide in which the semiconductor index fell about 12% and Nvidia around 9%, wiping roughly half a trillion dollars of market value. He said the sector had enjoyed an exceptionally strong run and that valuations had arguably become elevated. Even so, he believes the fundamentals remain strong, pointing to robust earnings growth.

Nvidia is his clearest example. Stickley said the chipmaker has clear visibility, a large order backlog and guidance for more than $100 billion in revenue next quarter, while its forward price-to-earnings ratio of around 11 times looks very cheap. He suggested setting aside the personal issues facing chief executive Jensen Huang and focusing on the business. He is not buying aggressively ahead of Nvidia’s results next week, he said, but he is starting to add exposure to the sector.

(Earlier: Mizuho’s Klein calls Nvidia ‘silly cheap’ below 10x earnings despite Huang uncertainty)

He cautioned that upcoming catalysts will test the AI investment case, particularly around the data centre rollout and the memory and chip suppliers at its core.

Closer to home, Stickley said Australian banks are holding up despite the cash rate rising to 4.85%, while consumer-facing companies are under pressure. His broader advice is to build positions gradually in high-quality names on pullbacks rather than trying to time the bottom.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Three drivers setting gold’s tone as December Fed hike bets build, according to Standard Chartered
item.description:
Gold’s drop on the CPI data shows how tightly the metal is now tied to Fed hike pricing, and therefore to oil. With a December quarter-point hike fully priced, any further rise in odds of a half-point move is likely to pressure bullion toward the support Standard Chartered has flagged, near $3,886. Equities are now a third driver: risk-off moves in stocks have not reliably supported gold during this conflict. The bank’s call for a softer dollar and steady central bank buying gives longer-term holders a reason to stay put, but the near-term path runs through December’s decision.

---

Fed speak is hawkish:

  • Fed’s Goolsbee calls CPI ‘borderline disturbing’, flags three inflation worries
  • Fed’s Paulson backs further gradual rate hikes, names three triggers for faster action
  • More from Fed’s Bowman: Shifts focus to inflation, wants AI and Middle East risks to ease first

---

Gold has kept its footing above $4,000, but with oil feeding Fed hike bets, Standard Chartered’s $4,700 target depends on a softer dollar arriving later rather than sooner.

Summary:

  • Standard Chartered said gold continues to trade above the key $4,000 level, with oil, inflation risks and equities setting the tone
  • Spot gold fell nearly 3% to around $4,020 on Tuesday after October CPI rose 0.4% month on month, against 0.3% expected
  • A December quarter-point Fed hike is fully priced, and half-point odds rose to around 10%
  • The bank stays overweight gold, with three-month and 12-month targets of $4,350 and $4,700
  • It expects Fed hikes in December and H1 2027 to a peak of 4.25% to 4.50%, and has flagged $3,886 as key support

Gold is still holding above the key $4,000 an ounce level despite a sharp sell-off after hotter-than-expected US inflation data, Standard Chartered said. Crude oil, inflation risks and equity markets are setting the tone, according to the bank, as traders focus on the Federal Reserve’s December meeting.

Spot gold fell nearly 3% on Tuesday to trade around $4,020 an ounce in the US session, while December futures dropped close to 2% to around $4,035. The metal had opened above $4,100 for the first time since October 22, but reversed after October consumer prices rose 0.4% on the month, above the 0.3% expected. The data lifted the dollar and Treasury yields, raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion.

Rate expectations shifted with the release. A quarter-point Fed hike in December is now fully priced, and the probability of a half-point move rose to around 10% from zero before the data, according to CME FedWatch. Fed Governor Christopher Waller had said earlier that a hot CPI reading could lead him to support a bigger increase.

Standard Chartered’s longer-term view remains constructive. In a report earlier this month, the bank said it remains overweight gold but trimmed its three-month target to $4,350 an ounce and its 12-month target to $4,700. It expects the Fed to raise rates in December and again in the first half of 2027, taking the target range to a peak of 4.25% to 4.50% before easing in the second half of next year. A softer dollar and continued buying by emerging-market central banks should drive gains over 12 months, it said, even though rising bond yields and a firmer dollar have been recent headwinds.

The bank has also flagged downside risk in the near term. In late October, it warned that gold needs to hold support around $3,886 after slipping below $4,000, or risk a deeper correction.

The pattern this year has been clear: rising oil prices from the Iran war have fed inflation and Fed hike expectations, and gold has struggled under that pressure rather than rallying as a haven. With December’s decision looming, oil and the next inflation data will decide whether the $4,000 floor holds. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
