item.title: SoftBank shares down after swings to $7 billion Q2 loss on $3.7 billion US data centre power hit
item.description:
The loss confirms that the cost of building AI infrastructure is now hitting the income statement, not just valuations, which adds to the wider debate about returns on AI spending. Record NAV and steady leverage limit balance-sheet concern. But the drop in pro forma NAV to around ¥44.7 trillion at November 9 prices shows how exposed SoftBank is to the recent tech sell-off. Any official OpenAI revaluation is the clearest potential positive catalyst for the shares. The data centre power writedown also adds to the evidence that power supply is a binding constraint on AI capacity growth, an issue also raised in UBS’s latest strategy note.

---

Posting ICYMI. SoftBank Group reported on Tuesday, November 10, after the Tokyo market close.

---

SoftBank paid up early for power to run AI data centres, and the bill has landed in its quarterly results, while the OpenAI upside is still waiting to be booked.

Summary:

  • SoftBank Group posted a fiscal Q2 net loss of about ¥1.12 trillion ($7 billion), against a ¥2.5 trillion profit a year earlier
  • A roughly $3.7 billion writedown on advance payments for US data centre power equipment was the largest hit, alongside Intel losses and higher financing costs
  • Revenue of ¥2.22 trillion beat the ¥2.02 trillion consensus
  • NAV reached a record ¥59.8 trillion at end-September, with LTV at 15.9%, but stood at about ¥44.7 trillion at November 9 prices
  • A further ¥3 trillion OpenAI investment lifted the stake to about 13%, and the new funding round valuation is not yet reflected

SoftBank Group swung to a net loss of about ¥1.12 trillion ($7 billion) in its fiscal second quarter, reversing a ¥2.5 trillion profit a year earlier, as a writedown on US AI data centre equipment, a fall in its Intel holding and higher financing costs weighed on results.

The biggest single hit was a roughly $3.7 billion (about ¥600 billion) writedown on nonrefundable advance payments for power-generation equipment intended for US data centres. A company executive said on the earnings call that SoftBank had made bridge investments early to secure the equipment in anticipation of shortages. Declines in investments including Intel and rising financing expenses added to the loss.

The top line was stronger. Revenue for the July to September quarter came in at ¥2.22 trillion, ahead of the LSEG consensus estimate of ¥2.02 trillion, supported by growth in telecommunications and AI computing.

For the first half of the fiscal year, SoftBank booked investment gains of about ¥1.7 trillion, down ¥2.2 trillion from a year earlier, leaving a net loss of around ¥770 billion for the six months.

The balance sheet tells a different story. Net asset value rose to a record ¥59.8 trillion at the end of September, up ¥20 trillion from the end of the last fiscal year. The loan-to-value ratio held at 15.9%, and the group kept about ¥5 trillion in liquidity. Recent market volatility has taken a toll, however: at November 9 prices, pro forma NAV stood at about ¥44.7 trillion.

OpenAI remains central to the investment case. SoftBank completed a further ¥3 trillion investment in the ChatGPT maker during the period, taking its stake to roughly 13%. It said any increase in OpenAI’s valuation from a new funding round has not yet been reflected in its results, pending an official announcement, which leaves potential upside for future quarters.

SoftBank also said this week that it would commit, together with Grab and Malaysia’s PETROS, a combined $1.85 billion in initial capital to develop AI infrastructure in Malaysia.

The results highlight the cost of SoftBank’s aggressive push into AI infrastructure. Investors will be watching the OpenAI revaluation and the group’s financing costs as the main swing factors in the second half.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australian investor home lending plunges 32% in Q3 as tax curbs and RBA hikes bite harder
item.description:
A drop in home lending this sharp gives the RBA more evidence that its five hikes this year are biting. That supports the case for a pause after November’s split decision, and it is a modest headwind for the Australian dollar. Short-dated Australian government bond yields may be sensitive to any further sign that housing is cooling faster than the central bank expects. Bank stocks face slower mortgage growth, especially in investor lending, which has traditionally been a profitable segment. With energy-driven inflation still the RBA’s main worry, oil prices remain the swing factor for whether housing weakness is enough to keep rates on hold.

-

Tax changes, lending caps and five rate hikes have all hit Australian property investors at once, and the result is a collapse in landlord borrowing.

Summary:

  • Australian home loan values fell 15.5% q/q in Q3, against expectations of an 8% drop and a 5.2% fall in Q2
  • Investor lending plunged 32.3%, after falling 10.2% in Q2
  • Owner-occupier loan values fell 5.3%, after a 1.9% fall in Q2
  • The May budget ended negative gearing for established homes bought after budget night and curbed the capital gains tax discount
  • APRA has capped high debt-to-income lending since February, and the RBA has hiked five times this year to 4.85%

The value of new Australian home loans fell 15.5% in the September quarter, nearly twice the 8% decline economists had expected, as lending to property investors collapsed in the wake of government tax changes and a year of Reserve Bank of Australia rate hikes.

Investor lending was the main drag, plunging 32.3% on the quarter after a 10.2% fall in the June quarter. Owner-occupier loan values fell a more modest 5.3%, following a 1.9% decline previously. The overall drop was a sharp acceleration from the 5.2% fall recorded in the prior quarter.

The split between investors and owner-occupiers suggests policy is doing much of the work. In the May federal budget, the government moved to end negative gearing for established homes bought after budget night, keeping it only for newly built properties, and also announced curbs to the capital gains tax discount on established dwellings. Negative gearing lets investors offset rental losses against other income. The government argued the housing market needed rebalancing, with most investor credit going towards existing homes rather than new supply. The major banks moved quickly to reflect the changes in how they assess investor loan applications, reducing borrowing capacity for many landlords.

Those measures came on top of tighter lending rules. From February, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority required banks to limit new loans at six or more times a borrower’s income to 20% of new mortgage lending, measured separately for owner-occupiers and investors.

Monetary policy has added further pressure. The RBA has raised its cash rate five times this year, in February, March, May, September and November, taking it to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, as it fights inflation that has been pushed higher by energy costs. The November decision was split 6-3, and the statement dropped earlier language about further increases.

The RBA’s own November Statement on Monetary Policy had already flagged a steep fall in investor lending, describing the drop in investor loan commitments as the largest in any hiking cycle on record. Governor Michele Bullock said a pullback in investor demand was normal in a housing downturn. The bigger fall compared with owner-occupiers, though, suggests the budget changes are having an effect.

The figures strengthen the case that housing is cooling quickly, which may feed into the RBA’s assessment of whether its tightening has gone far enough.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6855 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NIESR sees UK inflation above BoE target for four years, peaking at 4.4% in 2027
item.description:
A longer inflation overshoot driven by the Iran war’s energy shock keeps oil prices at the centre of the UK rate outlook: every sustained rise in crude raises the risk of further second-round effects on wages. NIESR’s call for only one more hike contrasts with market pricing of two or three. Its view that rates may need to reach around 5% points the other way, and supports the case for gilt yields and sterling to stay sensitive to energy-led data surprises. The critique of the October budget adds fiscal credibility risk on top, which could weigh on longer-dated gilts if borrowing plans keep slipping.

---

The Bank of England not the only one in deep doggy-doo:

  • Fed’s Goolsbee calls CPI ‘borderline disturbing’, flags three inflation worries

--- NIESR sees a longer inflation overshoot in Britain, and a BoE that may be doing less than the job requires.

Summary:

  • NIESR forecasts UK inflation will peak at 4.4% in February 2027, up from a 3.8% peak in its July forecast
  • It sees inflation above the BoE’s 2% target in 2027, 2028 and 2029, returning to target in late 2030
  • It expects one more BoE hike, in February, while markets price two or three by end-2027, and says rates may need to reach around 5%
  • The 2026 growth forecast is raised to 1.6% from 1.1%, slowing to 1.1% in 2027 and 0.9% in 2028
  • Unemployment is seen rising to a peak of 5.1% in 2031, with wage growth averaging 3.9% over three years
  • NIESR said the October budget did little to strengthen the public finances

UK inflation will stay above the Bank of England’s 2% target for the next four years as the Iran war’s energy shock feeds through into wages, the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) forecast on Tuesday. The think-tank also raised its outlook for growth.

It now expects inflation to peak at 4.4% in February 2027, up from the 3.8% peak it forecast in July. It sees inflation remaining above target through 2027, 2028 and 2029 before returning to 2% in late 2030, a year later than it previously expected. Second-round effects on wages are the main reason for the delay.

The outlook for policy is where NIESR parts company with markets. Investors are pricing two or three quarter-point rate hikes by the end of next year, but the think-tank expects the BoE to raise rates only once more, in February. NIESR also said rates would need to rise to around 5% to bring inflation back to target over the medium term, which suggests it thinks a single hike would not be enough to meet the goal on time. The BoE raised Bank Rate to 4% from 3.75% last week, its first increase in more than three years.

NIESR Director David Aikman said the economy had held up better than expected this year but now faces the twin pressures of higher energy prices and rising global borrowing costs. He said the policy response on both the monetary and fiscal sides is a domestic choice, and that decisions on both fronts are being put off.

On the fiscal side, NIESR said finance minister John Healey’s October budget did little to strengthen the public finances. Difficult decisions on tax and spending had largely been deferred, it said, and plans to reduce borrowing lacked credibility.

Growth has been more resilient than expected. NIESR raised its 2026 forecast to 1.6% from 1.1%, citing stronger government spending and business investment, partly driven by AI. It expects growth to slow to 1.1% in 2027 and 0.9% in 2028. Unemployment is projected to edge up from 4.8% in 2026 to a peak of 5.1% in 2031, with wage growth averaging 3.9% over the next three years.

The gap between NIESR’s single-hike forecast and market pricing will be tested at the BoE’s next meetings, with energy prices and wage settlements the key data to watch. 

---

NIESR is Britain’s longest-established independent economic research institute. It was founded in 1938 and is based in London. It is a non-profit charity, independent of government and political parties, and it publishes regular forecasts for the UK and global economies, which are widely watched alongside those from the Bank of England and the government’s fiscal watchdog. Its director, David Aikman, joined in 2023 from the Bank of England, where he worked on financial stability.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Goolsbee calls CPI ‘borderline disturbing’, flags three inflation worries
item.description:
Strong language like this from Goolsbee adds weight to the hawkish run of Fed commentary after the CPI report, and it strengthens pricing for a December hike. His focus on services and expectations points to concern about entrenched inflation, not transitory shocks, which raises the risk of a longer hiking cycle. That backdrop supports the US dollar and front-end Treasury yields, and remains a headwind for gold. With energy feeding the cost side of inflation, oil prices stay central to how hawkish the Fed may need to be.

---

Earlier:

  • Fed’s Paulson backs further gradual rate hikes, names three triggers for faster action
  • Fed's Bowman: Persistent inflation, firming labor conditions suggest 'work to do'

---

Goolsbee has gone from cautious to alarmed: sticky services prices and broad overheating make inflation a problem the Fed now has to confront.

Summary:

  • Goolsbee told PBS NewsHour that the October CPI report was borderline disturbing and that the US has a real inflation issue
  • He said the most troubling element is that services inflation is not coming down
  • He described inflation as driven by both cost and demand, and fears broad overheating across many prices
  • He said it would be a major concern if inflation gets built into expectations
  • The job market is steady and stable, he said, and everything is on the table to get inflation back to target

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee said Tuesday’s consumer price report was “borderline disturbing”, warning in an interview with PBS NewsHour that the US has a real inflation problem that policymakers will have to address.

Goolsbee said the most troubling element of the October data was that services inflation is not coming down. Services prices tend to reflect domestic demand and wage costs more than goods prices do. A lack of progress there suggests price pressures are becoming more entrenched rather than fading as one-off shocks unwind.

He described inflation as being driven from both the cost side and the demand side. His fear, he said, is the emergence of overheating across a broad range of prices, rather than increases confined to a few categories. At the same time, he noted that the job market remains steady and stable, which removes one of the usual arguments for holding back on tighter policy.

Goolsbee said a key concern would be inflation becoming built into expectations, and that the Fed would have to come to terms with it if price pressures stay persistent. He also pointed out that business investment is affected by interest rates, suggesting he is weighing how higher borrowing costs could feed through to spending. He stressed that everything is always on the table and that the Fed must bring inflation down to its target.

The interview added to a run of hawkish commentary from Fed officials after October’s CPI showed a larger-than-expected increase. Earlier on Tuesday, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said further gradual rate hikes seem appropriate, while Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said she was shifting her focus to inflation. Markets are pricing strong odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting.

Goolsbee’s choice of language stands out for an official who has often struck a more measured tone. With services inflation sticky and the labour market holding up, December’s decision will show how far policymakers are prepared to go to stop inflation becoming entrenched.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Paulson backs further gradual rate hikes, names three triggers for faster action
item.description:
Paulson’s comments add a voting member’s voice to the hawkish chorus after the hot CPI report, which reinforces pricing for a December hike and a follow-up in January. Her emphasis on gradual steps tempers the case for a half-point move, but her three triggers for faster action leave that door open if data keeps running hot. That combination supports the US dollar and front-end Treasury yields, while a firmer hiking path remains a headwind for gold. Because she names energy prices as an inflation driver, any further Middle East-driven gains in oil now feed directly into the Fed’s tightening calculus.

---

Earlier:

  • More from Fed’s Bowman: Shifts focus to inflation, wants AI and Middle East risks to ease first

---

Paulson favours steady hikes rather than sprints, but has set out exactly what would make her pick up the pace.

Summary:

  • Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson, a 2026 FOMC voter, said further gradual tightening seems appropriate
  • She said policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to return inflation to 2%, with underlying inflation stuck between 2.5% and 3%
  • She would favour moving faster if inflation expectations drift up, wage pressures build or underlying inflation rises
  • Paulson said the October CPI rise of 0.4% shows inflation pressures persist, driven by tariffs, energy and AI investment
  • Futures price strong odds of a quarter-point hike on December 8-9 from the current 3.75% to 4% range, and another in January

Philadelphia Federal Reserve President Anna Paulson said on Tuesday that further gradual interest rate increases appear appropriate to bring down elevated inflation, and that she would favour moving faster if price pressures worsen.

In the text of a speech prepared for a gathering in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania, Paulson said monetary policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to return inflation to the Fed’s 2% target. Inflation has run above that goal for more than five years, she noted, with underlying pressures holding between 2.5% and 3%. She said the exact path of rates will depend on how conditions evolve and that she will be watching the data closely.

Paulson, a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee this year, argued that a gradual approach has served the Fed well. In her view, it gives the economy time to adjust to higher borrowing costs while allowing policymakers room to assess the effects of their decisions. She said she has supported the Fed’s recent rate decisions and described bringing inflation down as her main priority, with the economy proving stronger than expected and the job market robust and stable.

She also set out the conditions under which she would favour a quicker pace. Paulson said she would want to act more quickly if inflation expectations drift higher, if wage pressures build, or if underlying inflation rises. She described risks to the inflation outlook as high and said the effects of AI and energy on prices are hard to gauge.

Her remarks came after October consumer price data showed a larger-than-expected rise, with the overall index up 0.4% on the month. Paulson said the report suggests inflation pressures remain very much present, pointing to tariffs, energy prices and AI investment as drivers. Economists saw signs that price increases once concentrated in a few areas are spreading more broadly.

Futures markets are pricing strong odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting, from the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, and a further increase in late January. Before the CPI release, Governor Christopher Waller said a reading like October’s could lead him to support a half-point move. The December meeting is now the key test of whether the Fed sticks with gradual steps or speeds up. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
